title: Kathmandu Valley UNESCO Sites: The 7 Monument Zones
meta_description: The 7 Kathmandu Valley UNESCO monument zones: what to see in each Durbar Square, stupa and temple, entry fees, 2015 earthquake restoration and etiquette.
summary: The Kathmandu Valley World Heritage Site, listed by UNESCO in 1979, has seven monument zones: the Durbar Squares of Kathmandu, Patan and Bhaktapur, the Buddhist stupas of Swayambhunath and Boudhanath, and the Hindu temples of Pashupatinath and Changu Narayan. All lie within 20 km of each other, and most were repaired after the 2015 earthquake.

sections.heading: One World Heritage Site, seven zones
paras: UNESCO inscribed the Kathmandu Valley on the World Heritage List in 1979 as a single site made of seven separate protected zones. Together they show how Hindu and Buddhist traditions grew side by side under the Licchavi kings from about the 5th century and the Malla kings from the 13th to 18th centuries, whose rival courts in Kathmandu, Patan and Bhaktapur competed through temples, palaces and festivals.

Rapid, unplanned building around the monuments put the site on UNESCO's List of World Heritage in Danger from 2003 to 2007, and the zone boundaries were redrawn in 2006 with stricter rules on new construction. That history still shapes a visit: modern concrete stands right at the edge of 17th-century squares, and the contrast is sharp.

The zones are close together. Patan Durbar Square is 6 km from Kathmandu Durbar Square, Bhaktapur 13 km east, and Changu Narayan on a ridge 6 km north of Bhaktapur. With a car and a guide, all seven fit into two full days; a third day lets you see them without rushing.

sections.heading: The three Durbar Squares
paras: Durbar means royal court, and each of the three old kingdoms built its palace square as a statement. Kathmandu's square, officially the Hanuman Dhoka zone, takes its name from the statue of the monkey god Hanuman by the palace gate. Inside are the Taleju temple of 1564, the 1757 Kumari Ghar where the living goddess lives, the Jagannath temple with carved roof struts, the 1908 neoclassical Gaddi Baithak and Kasthamandap, the wooden rest house that may have given Kathmandu its name.

Patan Durbar Square is the most complete of the three. The stone Krishna Mandir of 1637 faces a line of palace courtyards; Keshav Narayan Chowk now houses the Patan Museum, one of the best small museums in South Asia for bronze sculpture, and Sundari Chowk holds the carved Tusha Hiti royal bath. The 12th-century Golden Temple (Hiranya Varna Mahavihar), a Buddhist monastery courtyard, is a five-minute walk north.

Bhaktapur's zone covers three squares rather than one. Durbar Square has the Golden Gate of 1754 and the 55-Window Palace. Taumadhi Square has the Nyatapola, a five-storey pagoda of 1702 about 30 m tall and the tallest in Nepal, which survived both the 1934 and 2015 earthquakes. Dattatreya Square, the oldest part of town, has the carved Peacock Window.

sections.heading: Swayambhunath and Boudhanath stupas
paras: Swayambhunath sits on a wooded hill on the western edge of Kathmandu, at about 1,420 m. Its white dome and gilded tower, painted on four sides with the eyes of the Buddha, are among the oldest religious structures in the valley, with inscriptions from the 5th century. The eastern stairway of 365 steps is the pilgrims' route; monkeys on the hill gave the site its tourist name, the Monkey Temple. Around the stupa stand shrines, a Tibetan monastery and the Harati temple, sacred to Hindus and Buddhists alike.

Boudhanath, 7 km east, is one of the largest spherical stupas in the world, about 36 m high, on the old trade route to Tibet. After 1959 Tibetan refugees settled around it and built about 50 monasteries, so the area now feels like a Tibetan town. Its real life is the kora, the clockwise walk around the base, which is busiest at dawn and from about 4:30 pm. The spire was badly cracked in 2015, removed and rebuilt, and the stupa was reconsecrated in November 2016.

sections.heading: Pashupatinath and Changu Narayan
paras: Pashupatinath on the Bagmati River is Nepal's most sacred Hindu temple and one of the major Shiva shrines of the subcontinent. The main pagoda, with a two-tiered gilded roof and silver doors, enshrines the Pashupati lingam. Only Hindus may enter the inner courtyard; others watch from the terraces across the river. Along the ghats, cremations take place daily at Arya Ghat, while sadhus, small Shiva shrines and the deer park at Mrigasthali fill the eastern bank. Guhyeshwari, one of the Shakti Peethas, is a 15-minute walk downstream.

Changu Narayan, on a ridge at about 1,541 m, is the oldest temple site in the valley. A stone pillar by the west door carries an inscription of King Manadeva dated 464 CE, the oldest known in Nepal. The two-storey Vishnu pagoda itself was rebuilt in 1702 after a fire, and the courtyard is an open-air gallery of Licchavi stone carving, including Vishnu Vikranta striding across the universe and a kneeling Garuda. It is the quietest of the seven zones, with a small village street of shops and a private museum.

sections.heading: Entry fees and earthquake recovery by zone
paras: Each zone sells its own ticket, and Indian nationals pay the lower SAARC rate on showing a passport or voter ID. Fees fund conservation and are revised every few years, so check current status before you travel.

Tickets are checked at entry points on the main lanes, and again at random inside the zones, so keep them until you leave. A foreign visitor seeing all seven zones pays about NPR 5,700 in total. The Bhaktapur ticket can be extended for a week at the ticket office with your passport, which suits guests staying a night in the old town to see it at dawn and after dark.

sections.heading: The 2015 earthquake and the rebuilding
paras: On 25 April 2015 a magnitude 7.8 earthquake centred in Gorkha district, followed by a strong aftershock on 12 May, killed nearly 9,000 people in Nepal and damaged hundreds of historic buildings in the valley. In Kathmandu Durbar Square the Kasthamandap, the Trailokya Mohan Narayan temple and parts of the palace fell; in Patan and Bhaktapur, several temples on the squares came down to their plinths.

Nepal's Department of Archaeology led the recovery with local communities, guthis (traditional trusts) and international partners. Rebuilding followed the original methods where possible: carved timber struts were salvaged, numbered and reused, and new wood was carved by Newar craftsmen in Patan and Bhaktapur. Kasthamandap, rebuilt largely through community effort, was completed in 2021. A few structures remain under scaffolding, so photos taken before 2015 may not match what you see; check current status before you travel if a specific monument matters to you.

sections.heading: Etiquette at temples and stupas
paras: These are living places of worship, not museums. Daily puja, weddings, cremations and festivals take place around visitors, and a few habits keep everyone comfortable.
list: Walk clockwise around stupas, chortens and temples, and spin prayer wheels with your right hand
Remove shoes where you see others doing so, and leave leather belts and bags outside inner shrines where signs ask
Dress with shoulders and knees covered, especially at Pashupatinath and Changu Narayan
Do not photograph the Kumari when she appears at her window, and ask before photographing people at prayer
At Arya Ghat, watch cremations from the eastern bank, quietly and without close-up photos
Never touch offerings, step over them or climb on monuments and plinths
Drones are banned in all monument zones without written permission

faqs.q: What are the 7 UNESCO World Heritage Sites in Kathmandu?
faqs.a: The seven monument zones of the Kathmandu Valley World Heritage Site are Kathmandu Durbar Square (Hanuman Dhoka), Patan Durbar Square, Bhaktapur Durbar Square, Swayambhunath, Boudhanath, Pashupatinath and Changu Narayan. UNESCO lists them together as one site, inscribed in 1979. All lie within about 20 km of each other, and with a car and guide they can be seen in two full days.

Non-Hindus cannot enter the inner courtyard of the main Pashupatinath temple, and guards check at the gate. Foreign visitors pay about NPR 1,000 to visit the wider complex: the ghats, the eastern terraces facing the temple, smaller shrines and the Mrigasthali forest. Hindus of any nationality, including Indian pilgrims, can enter for darshan free of charge. Rules can change, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Was Kathmandu Durbar Square destroyed in the earthquake?
faqs.a: Kathmandu Durbar Square was badly damaged but not destroyed in the 25 April 2015 earthquake. Kasthamandap and the Trailokya Mohan Narayan temple collapsed, and parts of the palace were damaged. Many buildings survived, including the Taleju temple and the Kumari Ghar. Kasthamandap was rebuilt by 2021, and most of the square is open again, with some restoration still continuing.

faqs.q: Which Durbar Square is the best to visit?
faqs.a: If you can visit only one, choose Patan for its compact square, the Krishna Mandir and the Patan Museum, or Bhaktapur for its larger car-free old town and the five-storey Nyatapola temple. Kathmandu Durbar Square is the easiest to reach from Thamel and holds the Kumari Ghar. With two days in the valley, we include all three.

Swayambhunath is more than 1,500 years old. Inscriptions on the hill date to the 5th century CE, and legend places its origin even earlier, when the valley was a lake. The stupa has been rebuilt and regilded many times, most recently after the 2015 earthquake. Climb the 365-step eastern stairway in the morning for the pilgrim route and views across Kathmandu.

faqs.q: Is Boudhanath the largest stupa in Nepal?
faqs.a: Boudhanath is the largest stupa in Nepal and one of the largest spherical stupas in the world, about 36 m high. It sits on the old trade route to Tibet, and around 50 Tibetan monasteries surround it. After 2015 earthquake damage, its spire was rebuilt and the stupa reconsecrated in November 2016. Visit around 4:30 pm to join the evening kora.

faqs.q: Do I need separate tickets for each heritage site in Kathmandu?
faqs.a: Yes. Each of the seven monument zones charges its own entry fee; there is no combined valley pass. Foreigners pay from about NPR 200 at Swayambhunath to NPR 1,800 at Bhaktapur, and SAARC nationals pay much less. Keep each ticket during your visit, as checks happen inside the zones. Fees are revised periodically, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What is special about Changu Narayan temple?
faqs.a: Changu Narayan is the oldest temple site in the Kathmandu Valley. Its stone pillar carries a 464 CE inscription of King Manadeva, the oldest dated inscription in Nepal, and the courtyard holds some of the finest Licchavi stone sculpture. The two-storey Vishnu pagoda was rebuilt in 1702. It lies 6 km north of Bhaktapur and is far quieter than the other zones.

faqs.q: What should I wear to temples in Kathmandu?
faqs.a: Wear clothing that covers shoulders and knees, such as long trousers, long skirts or a kurta, at temples in Kathmandu. Choose shoes you can slip off easily, as many shrines ask you to remove them, and avoid leather belts where signs ask. A light scarf helps at Pashupatinath and Changu Narayan. Stupas are relaxed, but walk clockwise around them.
